This page goes with **Chapter 25, Sonata and Rondo Forms** of Robert Hutchinson's open textbook
[*Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom*](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/SonataAndRondoForms.html). Read each section
there first. These are the biggest forms in the book, so this page is a **listening-and-reading guide**: it tells you what to look for, and
sends you to real pieces in the site's [Analysed Scores Library](analysed-scores/view.qmd), where the score plays with the experts'
Roman-numeral key labels under it. The key plans below are read from that analysis data. Bar numbers are approximate (the data puts key
changes at beat positions); open the piece and listen for each change.

## 25.1 The plan of a sonata form

Sonata form (also called first-movement form) is the main plan of Classical and later first movements. It has three large parts and
the book shows a standard layout:

| Part | What happens | Key (major-key piece) |
|---|---|---|
| **Exposition** | **primary theme** (PT) in the tonic, a **transition** that moves away, a **secondary theme** (ST), then often a closing theme | PT in I, ST in **V** |
| **Development** | themes fragmented and sequenced, passing through several keys | unstable |
| **Recapitulation** | the same material again, now with the ST **brought into the tonic** | I throughout |

[Read 25.1](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/SonataAndRondoForms.html)

Many pieces have two secondary themes, or no closing theme, or a development that brings in new material. In a Classical score the exposition
is repeated, and the development and recapitulation are repeated together: a **two-reprise** form, a descendant of balanced and rounded binary
([Chapter 24](binary-ternary.qmd)). **Sonatina form** is a sonata form with no development section; the book's example is the "Miniature
Overture" from Tchaikovsky's *Nutcracker*.

**Try it with a real piece.** Open Mozart's
[Piano Sonata K. 545, movement 1](analysed-scores/view.qmd?id=mozart-sonata-16-1) (the "Sonata facile"). The analysis labels its keys in
this order: **C major**, **G major**, then **G minor, D minor, A minor**, **F major**, and finally **C major** again. Match them to the plan:

- C major is the primary theme and transition; **G major** (about bar 13) is the secondary theme, in the dominant;
- the move to **G minor** (about bar 29) is the start of the development, which passes through D minor and A minor;
- the **F major** label (about bar 41) is the beginning of the recapitulation, and **C major** (about bar 51) is the point where the
  secondary theme arrives *in the tonic*.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## What to notice

The recapitulation of K. 545 begins in F major (the subdominant) rather than the tonic, a famous quirk. The "home" feeling arrives only
when the secondary theme returns in C. That is **sonata principle** (25.2): the piece is not finished until the music that was in the
"wrong" key at the start is heard in the home key.
:::

## 25.2 Sonata principle and the monothematic sonata

**Sonata principle** is Charles Rosen's idea that the key of the second theme is a large-scale **dissonance** that the piece must resolve:
material first stated outside the tonic is restated in the tonic. It is why a recapitulation re-writes the transition so it stays at home.
In a **monothematic** sonata (Haydn's favourite), the primary theme reappears in the dominant where a new secondary theme would be, so the
key plan carries the drama by itself.
[Read 25.2](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/SonataAndRondoForms.html)

## 25.3 Four structural functions

Peter Temko and Peter Spencer label music by what it *does*, not what it is called. The same bit of a movement can be assigned a function by
asking four questions:

| Function | Sounds like | Where it is typical |
|---|---|---|
| **Expository** | a stable key, clear melodies, well-formed phrases with cadences | primary and secondary themes, binary and ternary pieces |
| **Transitional** | moving to a new key, more active texture, often ending on a half cadence and a rest | between PT and ST, retransitions |
| **Developmental** | sequences, fragments of themes, many keys, irregular phrase lengths | the development |
| **Terminative** | emphatic back-and-forth between tonic and dominant to confirm the key | closing theme, coda |

[Read 25.3](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/SonataAndRondoForms.html)

**Practise on K. 545 above.** Play it and label stretches: the first four bars (expository, a theme with a cadence); the stretch after it that
leaves C (transitional: look for the chord that closes it just before the secondary theme); the section in G minor, D minor and A minor
(developmental); the last bars of the exposition (terminative). The library's Roman numerals show the V and I chords alternating in
terminative music.

## 25.4 Rondo forms

A **rondo** alternates a **refrain** (A) with **episodes** (B, C). A **five-part** rondo is A B A C A (or A B A B A), a **seven-part** rondo A B A C
A B A. The refrain is always in the tonic. The first episode is in a closely related key (the dominant in a major piece, the relative
major, III, in a minor one); the second episode ranges more widely (the tonic minor, the submediant, the subdominant). A **retransition**
is a passage that leads back to music already heard. Hearing the first episode first away from the tonic and later in it is another sonata
principle at work.
[Read 25.4](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/SonataAndRondoForms.html)

**Hear a five-part rondo.** Beethoven's Piano Sonata Op. 49 No. 2 ends with a
[Tempo di Menuetto](analysed-scores/view.qmd?id=beethoven-sonata-20-2) (the library's "movement 2"). Its key labels are **G major, D major,
G major, C major, G major**. In the plan the refrain (A, in G) is followed by an episode in the **dominant** (B, at about bar 20), the refrain, a
second episode in the **subdominant** (C, at about bar 51), and the refrain again: **A B A C A**. Check it: does the tune that opens the
piece come back each time the key returns to G?

**Another rondo to read.** Mozart's
[K. 545, movement 3](analysed-scores/view.qmd?id=mozart-sonata-16-3) is a rondo too; its labels run C major, G major, C major, A minor, C major.
Try to say which stretches are refrain and which are episodes, and which of the refrain's returns is shortened. (This one is for
listening; the form is not as clean as the Beethoven.)

**A five-part rondo you can read bar by bar: Beethoven, *Für Elise*.** The full-score player has it
([open the score](analysed-scores/full-scores.qmd?id=pdmx-254); a community score, bar numbers count the pickup as bar 1). The notes give this plan:

| Bars | Section | What the notes show |
|---|---|---|
| 1-24 | **A** (refrain) | the famous tune in A minor, a period (see [13.9](phrases-in-combination.qmd)), then a second idea in bars 11-14 (chords C, G, A minor, E) that leads back to the tune |
| 25-40 | **B** (episode) | the melody has B♭ in it from bar 26, so it leaves A minor for F major, and it ends with a few bars on the opening notes leading back |
| 41-62 | **A** | the refrain again, built from music already heard: bars 41-48 are bars 17-24 and bars 49-60 are bars 11-22 |
| 63-84 | **C** (episode) | slow chords instead of the running figure (bars 63-79), then an ascending run through bars 80-84 into the refrain |
| 85-106 | **A** | the refrain once more, note for note the same as bars 41-61 |

That is **A B A C A**, the book's five-part plan. The key names for B and C are read from the accidentals and are **unverified**; check them with the
score and your ears. Notice what a rondo can do with a *retransition*: bars 37-40 and 80-84 are both short passages that lead back to the refrain.

**A refrain with an unusual shape: Beethoven, Sonatina in F, Anh. 5 No. 2, Rondo.** ([open the score](analysed-scores/full-scores.qmd?id=pdmx-429)).
The refrain is the first eighteen bars (see [13.9](phrases-in-combination.qmd) on why it is a phrase chain), and the movement returns to its opening
figure in bars 19-20 and again from bar 51. I did not map the whole movement, so it stays an item to read.

**The book's seven-part rondo: Beethoven, *Pathétique* Sonata, III.** This movement is not in the score player (see the note below), so there is no
score to open. Its plan here was read from the notes of the public-domain Mutopia edition (typeset in LilyPond, played out as MIDI, and
compared bar against bar by a script, `scripts/mutopia/midi-structure.py`). It has 210 bars in 2/2 with a short upbeat before bar 1. The key names come from
a pitch-class count over each stretch, so treat them as a guide to listen with (**unverified**):

| Bars | Section | What the notes show |
|---|---|---|
| 1-16 | **A** (refrain) | C minor, a melody over a rolling accompaniment |
| 17-24 | transition | leaves C minor, then G minor |
| 25-56 | **B** (first episode) | around E♭ major (with B♭ and A♭ on the way): the relative major, as the book says. The tune of bars 37-42 comes back in bars 147-152, note for note but 3 semitones lower, which is E♭ going down to C |
| 57-60 | retransition | G (the dominant), leading back to the refrain |
| 61-72 | **A** | the refrain again: bars 62-64 are bars 1-3, and bars 67-78 are bars 6-17 |
| 73-106 | **C** (second episode) | moves to A♭ major from about bar 81 (the submediant, the book's second-episode key), with E♭ and F minor on the way |
| 107-120 | retransition | about fourteen bars centred on G, the dominant |
| 121-136 | **A** (short) | the refrain's opening (bars 121-123) and then, within the next bars, only part of it |
| 137-158 | **B** | the first episode's tune, now in **C major** (the tonic, and the sonata-principle move) |
| 159-170 | retransition | short sequences on the last motives of the episode, then the refrain |
| 171-182 | **A** | the last refrain (bars 171-173 and 176-177 match bar 1-3 and 6-7) |
| 183-210 | coda | C minor with a few C major bars, ending in C minor |

That is **A B A C A B A** with a coda: the book's seven-part rondo. Note how it follows **sonata principle**: B first stands in E♭, away from the tonic, and then
in the tonic, as the second theme does in a sonata.

**Sonata form to read from the notes: Beethoven, *Moonlight* Sonata, III (Presto agitato).** Also read from a Mutopia edition (CC BY-SA 2.5); the same method,
201 bars in the MIDI (a bar more than the printed count, probably from the repeat's alternative endings; treat bar numbers as a guide). It is in C♯ minor.

| Bars | Part | What the notes show |
|---|---|---|
| 1-18 | exposition: primary theme | the arpeggio theme in C♯ minor; the opening bar comes back at bar 15 |
| about 19-64 | exposition: transition, secondary group, closing | the key region moves to the dominant side (G♯ / D♯ by pitch count). Bars 19-30 are the first material in the new key |
| 65-102 | development | a long section moving through several keys; no return of the primary theme until bar 103 |
| 103-114 | recapitulation: primary theme | bars 103-106 are bars 1-4 note for note |
| 115-164 | recapitulation: secondary group | bars 115-126 are bars 19-30 again, **a fifth lower**: the music that stood in the dominant region now stands in the tonic |
| about 165-201 | coda | back to the primary theme and the tonic |

The fifth-lower recurrence (bars 19-30 and 115-126, checked by comparing the notes) is the sonata principle in one line of data. The exact bar where the exposition's
second theme begins is not marked here, because the pitch count can't tell a transition from a new theme; use the score and your ears.

**Why these two are not in the score player.** The player needs MusicXML, and the PDMX conversions of these sonatas failed. The Mutopia editions came as
LilyPond only. A direct MusicXML conversion dropped notes, so it was not used (details in `research_notes/pdmx-conversion.org`). Sources: Mutopia Project,
*Pathétique* III (public domain) and *Moonlight* III (Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 2.5), both after the Berners 1908 edition edited by Winterberger.

## 25.5 Sonata rondo and rondo character

**Sonata rondo** replaces the second episode with a development: **A B A development A B A**. The B section appears first in the dominant
and then in the tonic, as in sonata form. **Rondo character** means a quick, light, duple-metre movement (simple or compound) with staccato
touches, and it is the usual character of a Classical finale. The book's detailed rondo walk-through is Beethoven's *Pathétique*, III (a
seven-part rondo in C minor, with the first episode in E♭ major, the second in the submediant, and the first episode coming back in C major); its plan is in 25.4 above.
[Read 25.5](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/SonataAndRondoForms.html)

## 25.6 Forms in a whole sonata

The book ends with the usual movements of a Classical multimovement work (a first movement in sonata form, a slow movement in a binary,
ternary or sonata plan, then a minuet and trio and a rondo or sonata-rondo finale). You can see all of these in the library: pick one
Mozart or Beethoven sonata and open its movements one after another.

- **Sonata K. 545:** [movement 1](analysed-scores/view.qmd?id=mozart-sonata-16-1) (sonata form), [movement 2](analysed-scores/view.qmd?id=mozart-sonata-16-2) (ternary, see Chapter 24), [movement 3](analysed-scores/view.qmd?id=mozart-sonata-16-3) (rondo).
- **Beethoven Op. 2 No. 1:** [movement 1](analysed-scores/view.qmd?id=beethoven-sonata-1-1) (sonata form in F minor: the labels show A♭ major in the exposition and F minor again at the recapitulation) and [movement 3](analysed-scores/view.qmd?id=beethoven-sonata-1-3) (minuet and trio).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## For teachers

- **Where the key plans come from:** the Analysed Scores Library's analysis data (Mozart: DCML annotators; Beethoven: BPS dataset), read in
  order. Bar numbers on this page are approximate and not checked against a printed score. The recapitulation-in-the-subdominant remark about
  K. 545 and the Op. 49 No. 2 rondo reading are from the key labels plus general knowledge of the pieces; the book does not analyse these two.
- **The book's own pieces** (Mozart K. 333 and K. 284, Haydn Hob. XVI:35, Beethoven *Moonlight* III and *Pathétique* III, Mozart's *Eine kleine
  Nachtmusik* II) are not all in the library. *Moonlight* I is; *Moonlight* III and *Pathétique* III are read from Mutopia MIDI exports instead (25.4).
- **Not here:** drills. Form recognition in sonata and rondo form depends on listening, and a computer cannot yet generate a sonata
  exposition to ask about. A Timestamp Notes outline of one movement is the cheapest way to get a class to mark its sections
  ([Timestamp Notes](../tools/timestamp-notes.qmd)).
- The text on this page is written for the site, not copied from the book (the book is under the GNU Free Documentation License).
:::
